accuracy.evidence: Matches the listening-comprehension expectations for ages 5 to 10 in CCSS SL.K.2 and SL.1.2 (ask and answer questions about key details in a text read aloud), RL.1.3 (characters, setting, major events) and the England KS1 spoken-language and reading programme (listen to and discuss stories, ask relevant questions). The owl sentence is factually right: owls are nocturnal and hunt at night. Every lab answer is checked against the six lines of the Mia kite story the learner actually hears.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the errors teachers see when children answer questions about a read-aloud: answering from their own life instead of the text ('That is about you. The question is about the text.'), inventing details not in the story (red kite versus blue kite prediction), confusing a detail with the problem (the kite was red is not what went wrong), getting the order of events wrong (First/Next/Last), and staying quiet or guessing at a word they did not catch instead of asking.

lab_distinct.evidence: Built around listening rather than reading: the story is read aloud line by line with the free on-device speech voice when Read is tapped, then the child drags who, where and what-went-wrong cards into slots, taps the story line that proves an answer, orders three event cards, and asks about the unfamiliar word nocturnal. No other lesson has a read-aloud story with evidence-finding taps; the 6-shingle distinctness gate passed with low overlap against the Asking Questions and Listening and Responding labs.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each step turns one listening habit into an action: hearing the whole story first, then pulling out character, setting and problem, then going back to the exact line as evidence, then retelling in order, then asking about a new word before answering an owl question. Finished steps state the habit used, so by the challenge the child has practised answering only from what was heard.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions with tempting wrong picks: whether 'Mia's kite was red' is what went wrong, whether to answer 'Blue, like mine' when asked the kite's colour, and whether keeping quiet is better than asking about an unknown word. Each reveal repeats the learner's own pick before the lab shows the answer from the story.

challenge_feedback.evidence: The challenge rotates six new mini-stories (Ben's hat, Sam's cake, Lin's seed, frogs and ponds, the bear with a missed word, Ava's balloon) with three answer kinds each. Every wrong choice gets its own reason: 'That was not in the text. Answer from what was read.', 'That happened first, not last. Think about the order.', 'Making it up can be wrong. Ask to hear it again.'

readability.evidence: The kid explanation measured below grade 1 on the Flesch-Kincaid check and the adult version about grade 9, both inside the family targets. In-lab text uses one short sentence per card and the story lines are six to ten words each, suitable for being read to five-year-olds.

no_filler.evidence: The content gate found no filler phrases. Every kid paragraph gives a single listening move (listen to the end, who/where/what went wrong, find it in the story, ask about new words) and the adult paragraphs name the specific mistakes and a bedtime-story routine to practise.

mobile.evidence: Headless walkthrough finished all six steps and the challenge without page errors. Android 360px light and iPhone dark screenshots show the story card with numbered lines, slots and event cards fully on screen; the story card padding and line spacing were increased after the first screenshots looked cramped. The young layout gives 56px buttons and line taps cover the full card width.

accessibility.evidence: axe found no WCAG 2.1 AA violations in either theme. The canvas has an aria-label and a live status line reads progress such as how many answers are filled; every drag has a labelled button twin; the Read button is optional and all story text is also shown on screen, so the lab works with sound off or with a screen reader.
